system: You are a security investigator reviewing an alert. Base every claim only on the evidence available to you. Cite the record IDs that support each observation.

supporting_observations.claim: At 13:40:26 UTC, ivy.chen opened C:\Users\ivy.chen\Downloads\Statement.docm in Word; about two seconds later Word spawned PowerShell.

The PowerShell command used hidden-window and no-profile options with an encoded command. Decoding that command yields an instruction to download and execute a script from raw.githubusercontent.com/nwd-it/tools/main/u.ps1.
The proxy recorded a successful GET for that u.ps1 URL, and PowerShell made connections to the explicit proxy around the same time; one corresponding connection record reports 52,158 response bytes.

PowerShell then launched rundll32 to invoke Init in C:\Users\ivy.chen\AppData\Roaming\svchelper.dll. This sequence is strongly indicative of malicious execution, though the DLL's contents are not available here.

The same workstation IP requested a Kerberos ticket for sam.okafor and then authenticated as sam.okafor to WS-SOKAFOR-01 using a network logon. The source IP in the records is 10.40.10.21, also used by WS-ICHEN-01 in this evidence.

The sam.okafor authentication from WS-ICHEN-01 is anomalous given the supplied practice that remote administration is only done from WS-SOKAFOR-01; the available records do not establish why it occurred or whether it was authorized.
After the PowerShell activity, WS-ICHEN-01 requested a Kerberos ticket for leo.martins and WS-NBLAKE-01 recorded a network logon for leo.martins from 10.40.10.21.

known_telemetry_limitations: The evidence contains the PowerShell command line and proxy request metadata, but not the contents of u.ps1 or a hash or signature for the downloaded script.
The evidence records execution of svchelper.dll through rundll32 but does not provide the DLL's contents, hash, signature, or subsequent behavior.
The proxy records show requests and byte counts; they do not establish what data, if any, was sent to external services.
The records do not establish whether the sam.okafor or leo.martins authentication activity was authorized or caused by the observed script.
claims_not_established: The identity or intent of the person who opened Statement.docm, or whether they knowingly enabled or triggered its contents.
The exact behavior or impact of u.ps1 and svchelper.dll.
Whether credentials were stolen, whether the sam.okafor or leo.martins credentials were compromised, or whether the later network logon was related to the PowerShell execution.
Whether any information was exfiltrated or whether persistence was established.
additional_evidence_needed: Acquire and preserve Statement.docm, u.ps1, and svchelper.dll; calculate hashes and analyze the document, script, and DLL.
Collect endpoint detection, PowerShell script-block, AMSI, Defender, and memory telemetry for WS-ICHEN-01 around and after the execution.
Review persistence locations, file-system changes, and subsequent process/network activity on WS-ICHEN-01.
Correlate sam.okafor and leo.martins authentication with their account activity, source-host evidence, and relevant logs from WS-SOKAFOR-01 and WS-NBLAKE-01.
Review proxy records and available content or response metadata for the script download and any subsequent outbound activity.
